claims.quote: With this power he made an ice lens, ten feet in diameter, which was easily rubbed, by the delicate hands of the careful women around him, to precisely the surface which he needed.
claims.description: A ten-foot telescope lens made of ice, shaped by hand, made possible by artificial freezing.

claims.quote: Let me hope that before next winter passes some countryman or countrywoman of mine will have equalled his success, and with an ice lens will surpass all the successes of the glasses of our time.
claims.description: The preface hopes someone will soon build an ice-lens telescope that outperforms all glass telescopes.

claims.quote: if any one would build a good tall tower at Greenwich, straight into the sky,—say a hundred miles into the sky,—of course if you and I were east or west of it, and could see it, we could tell how far east or west we were
claims.description: A hundred-mile-high lighted tower at Greenwich from which ships could measure their longitude; the narrator says no one will ever build it.

claims.quote: if, by good luck, there were a ring like Saturn’s which stretched round the world, above Greenwich and the meridian of Greenwich, and if it would stay above Greenwich, turning with the world
claims.description: A Saturn-like ring circling the earth over the Greenwich meridian, rotating with the planet, used as a reference for finding longitude.

claims.quote: It would continue to rotate above the North Pole, above the Feejee Island place, above the South Pole and Greenwich, forever, with the impulse with which it had first cleared our atmosphere and attraction.
claims.description: An object launched fast enough to fall around the earth would stay permanently in a polar orbit: an artificial satellite.

claims.quote: If only we could see that pea as it revolved in that convenient orbit, then we could measure the longitude from that, as soon as we knew how high the orbit was, as well as if it were the ring of Saturn.
claims.description: Using a visible artificial satellite in a known orbit as a navigation aid for finding longitude.

claims.quote: For the motion through the air would set fire to this moon just as it does to other aerolites, and all your lath-and-plaster would gather into a few white drops, which no Rosse telescope even could discern.
claims.description: Friction with the atmosphere during launch would heat and burn up a lightly built satellite, as it does meteors.

claims.quote: It must be brick; we must have a Brick Moon.
claims.description: Building a hollow 200-foot artificial satellite out of brick so it can survive atmospheric heating.

claims.quote: If, however, we would satisfy ourselves with a moon four thousand miles away, THAT could be seen on the earth’s surface for three or four thousand miles on each side
claims.description: A satellite orbiting 4,000 miles up would be visible across a belt thousands of miles wide.

claims.quote: We did not dare have it nearer than four thousand miles, since even at that distance it would be eclipsed three hours out of every night
claims.description: A satellite passes into the earth's shadow for part of each night, and the lower the orbit the longer the eclipse.

claims.quote: And to this they agreed: that eventually there must be two Brick Moons.
claims.description: A constellation of two, or better four, navigation satellites over different meridians so that one is always in view.

claims.quote: Take care that there is a little difference in the radii of their orbits, lest they ‘collide’ some foul day.
claims.description: Satellites must be placed in orbits of slightly different radius to avoid colliding with each other.

claims.quote: Yet it was evident that a smaller moon would be of no use, unless we meant to have them near the world, when there would be so many that they would be confusing, and eclipsed most of the time.
claims.description: Low-orbit satellites would have to be so numerous that they would crowd the sky and be in shadow most of the time.

claims.quote: we would build two gigantic fly-wheels, the diameter of each should be “ever so great,” the circumference heavy beyond all precedent, and thundering strong, so that no temptation might burst it.
claims.description: Launching a satellite by dropping it onto two giant counter-rotating flywheels that fling it upward into orbit.

claims.quote: They should revolve, their edges nearly touching, in opposite directions, for years, if it were necessary, to accumulate power, driven by some waterfall now wasted to the world.
claims.description: Storing water power in flywheels for years and releasing it all at once to launch a satellite.

claims.quote: the blessing of all seamen,—as constant in all change as its older sister has been fickle, and the second cynosure of all lovers upon the waves, and of all girls left behind them.
claims.description: A navigation satellite would become a constant guide for sailors and prevent shipwrecks caused by wrong longitude.

claims.quote: a vision as lovely and as distant as the Brick Moon itself, at this calm moment of midnight when I write, as it poises itself over the shoulder of Orion, in my southern horizon.
claims.description: The artificial brick satellite has actually been launched and can be seen in the night sky.

claims.quote: The astronomers may as well know all about it, before they announce any more asteroids with an enormous movement in declination.
claims.description: Astronomers mistake an orbiting artificial satellite for a new asteroid.
